items.stem: Why are default configurations a security risk?

options.text: Defaults favour easy setup and are widely known to attackers
options.rationale: Correct: well-known defaults (accounts, ports, settings) are easy targets.

options.text: Defaults are encrypted and cannot be read
options.rationale: Defaults are published and well known, not hidden.

options.text: Defaults always meet every compliance standard

items.stem: Which TWO actions reduce a system's attack surface? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Disable services and ports the system does not need
options.rationale: Correct: fewer running services means fewer entry points.

options.text: Remove or disable default and unused accounts
options.rationale: Correct: default accounts are common attack targets.

options.text: Enable every optional feature by default
options.rationale: More features means more attack surface.

options.text: Keep sample accounts active for convenience
options.rationale: Sample accounts are a known weakness.

items.stem: What is configuration drift and why does it matter?

options.text: Gradual divergence from the baseline that reopens vulnerabilities over time
options.rationale: Correct: unmanaged changes erode the hardened state.

options.text: A one-time setting that never changes
options.rationale: Drift is change over time, not a fixed setting.

options.text: A type of network cable fault
options.rationale: Drift here refers to configuration, not cabling.
